subject: A new Washington-Beijing compact
posts:
When superpowers forge a new compact around trade machinery and summitry, who secures stability and who gets sidelined?
Evidence: red carpet welcome, board of trade, tariff machinery
#Aletheia #Geopolitics

Xi's Washington visit establishes a stable bilateral compact through regular summitry, negotiated differences, and mutual recognition of power.
Stated Judgement: (+0.8, +0.5) — Good Preference

Behind institutional trade bodies lie stark strategic competition and bilateral carve-outs that frequently bypass regional allies like Australia.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.2, -0.3) — Lesser Evil

Verdict: COND — The Path of Deception.
The compact stabilizes superpower friction through managed trade mechanisms while sidelining third-party allies.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.4, z: 1)

- Geoff Raby / Analysis: COND (-0.1, -0.2) — Examines bilateral institutional resets.
- US-China Compact: COND (-0.2, -0.3) — Manages tariffs and rare earths supply chains.
Presidents Trump and Xi formalized a new bilateral framework including a Board of Trade and Investment to manage tariffs, rare earths, and supply chains.

The Bright Side:
Institutionalized economic channels reduce the risk of catastrophic trade warfare.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The analysis treats administrative trade machinery (HOW) as proof of permanent systemic harmony (WHY).

Social Physics Analysis:
Superpower actors operate via smart self-interested accommodation. They construct bilateral negotiation channels to lock in advantage while insulating themselves from wider multilateral fallout.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Deception. F_pos vs F_neg forces reflect pragmatic management.

The Unavoidable Truth: Bilateral superpower compacts prioritize core national interests over regional allies.
The Unavoidable Lie: Institutional trade boards eliminate underlying geopolitical rivalry.

Alethekanon:
Realist accommodation between giants creates stability for themselves while imposing strategic discipline on everyone else.

Awwthekanon:
It is a relief when great nations choose negotiation over conflict, sparing millions from the shadow of economic ruin. May their talks yield genuine care for the wider world.

Brothekanon:
They rolled out a 30-meter red carpet and set up trade boards. Turns out superpowers prefer cutting deals directly rather than listening to everyone else.

Spirithekanon:
"If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all." Romans 12:18 PASS
Pragmatic pacts between rivals avert ruin, even if driven by self-interest.

Actual Article Body:
September 29, 2026

Xi Jinping’s Washington visit was more than ceremony and trade deals. The US and China are building a more stable relationship around regular summitry, negotiated differences and mutual recognition of power. Australia needs to understand what has changed.

Last week, on the tarmac of Andrews Air Force Base in Washington, a key moment in global affairs occurred. Not since JFK met Harold Macmillan in 1962 had a US president welcomed a visiting head of state at the airport. The symbolism was as profound as it was considered. Through that gesture the US president was acknowledging that China was a co-equal power with the United States.

It must have been particularly satisfying to President Xi. His presidency will be seen as one during which China rose from being a significantly weaker, challenging, ascendant power, to being acknowledged by the US as its equal. If Xi is looking for a legacy, this will surely be sitting on the mantelpiece.

The Washington meeting was the culmination of a reset in US/China bilateral relations that began in earnest last November at the Busan APEC leaders’ meeting. Trump flew to Busan and met only with Xi and then turned his back on the rest of the gathered leaders, announcing that he had just had a ‘G2’ meeting with Xi and looked forward to future meetings.

That meeting agreed on the ‘Busan Pause’ or the tariff truce. In May this year Trump visited Beijing and announced progress on one of the administration’s key priorities: tougher Chinese action against the fentanyl trade. The intention to establish a Board of Trade and a Board of Investment were also announced.

With the just-concluded Washington meeting, the media focus on ‘deliverables’ was understandable. But the US and Australian media covering Xi’s visit seem to have written their stories before it began.

The most predictable and ubiquitous headlines were different variants of the ‘all form but no substance’ theme. Some journalists even feigned deep surprise that many issues remained over which the US and China still differed.

It has taken some days, but both the US and China have now released their official accounts of the outcomes from the meetings. While the accounts from both sides are largely consistent with each other, not surprisingly emphases and some points differ.

The US statement highlighted the agreement over tougher Chinese enforcement of controls over opiates and other substances, noting recent arrests by Chinese authorities based on cooperation with US anti-narcotics agencies and the ‘operationalising’ of the Board of Trade.

The Board of Trade will recommend tariff cuts for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. The US expects this to lead to increased exports to China of agricultural goods, fish and seafood, lumber, cosmetics and medical devices.

Agreement was also reached for China to import an additional 10 million tonnes of metallurgical coal from the US, something the Australian media has ignored, despite its likely harm to Australia’s own interests.

A Board of Investment will also be established to explore potential investment opportunities, identify impediments to investment and provide a ‘structured channel’ for both sides to address ‘investment-related’ issues. This is something that the Australian Government would be well advised to study to see its possible relevance for Australia-China investment relations. Again, the Australian media has not reported on this.

According to the US, both sides have agreed to address US concerns over the supply of rare earths and related supply chains. And the US has requested China to increase production of refined petroleum product to stabilise global supply.
